reading.rtitle: Project Atlas: Recommendation Following Legal Due Diligence
paras: This memo summarizes the findings of the legal due diligence on Ribeira Software and sets out our recommendation to the board. The bottom line is simple: the acquisition remains attractive, but not at the current price and not on the current terms. The reason is a single item that did not appear in the seller's disclosure: an unresolved tax claim against the company's Brazilian subsidiary, with a potential exposure of approximately four million dollars.

The claim came to light during our review of the subsidiary's correspondence with the tax authority, not through any disclosure by the seller. The seller's explanation is that the claim was considered unlikely to succeed and therefore immaterial. We do not share that assessment. Its omission from the disclosure schedule is, at best, an oversight; at worst, it raises a question about the reliability of the seller's other warranties.

Our recommendation is not withdrawal from the transaction. Withdrawal at this stage would mean the loss of eight months of work and of a strategic position in the market. Instead, we propose three changes to the terms: a reduction in the purchase price of two million dollars; the retention of a further four million dollars in escrow until the final resolution of the claim; and a specific indemnity from the seller covering any liability arising from it. The closing date would move from March to May to allow for the renegotiation.

Two caveats apply. First, our estimate of the exposure is based on the documents available to us and is contingent on the accuracy of the tax authority's calculation. Second, the seller's willingness to accept these terms is uncertain, and there is a real likelihood of resistance on the escrow. Our advice is nonetheless to err on the side of caution: a deal that survives these conditions is worth signing, and a deal that does not was never worth the price.

listenings.text: When a junior lawyer sends me a memo, I look for one thing in the first paragraph, and that is the recommendation. If I have to reach page two to find out what you want me to do, the memo has already failed. Written English for a board is built out of nouns: the acquisition, the review, the recommendation, the reduction in price. That is not decoration. A noun lets you pack a whole event into two words and put it at the front of the sentence, where the reader can find it. But the same density that works on the page fails out loud. If you stand up in a meeting and say, following the completion of our review, our recommendation is a reduction in the price, people stop listening by the fourth noun. So when you present the memo, turn the nouns back into verbs. We reviewed the accounts. We found a claim. We think the price should come down. Same content, half the effort for the people in the room.

I have read hundreds of memos in my career, and I remember about three of them. The one I remember best was two pages long. The first line said: we recommend going ahead, subject to three conditions. By the end of the first page I knew the price, the risk, and what it would cost to protect ourselves. The seller hated the escrow. They threatened to walk away twice, and our own sales director wanted to give in. In the end they accepted three million in escrow instead of four, and we closed in May instead of March. Eighteen months later, the tax claim was settled for almost exactly that amount. If that memo had been ten pages of background, I would have signed in March, and the claim would have been our problem instead of theirs.

extra_audio.text: First, the legal team reviews the target company's documents, including its correspondence with the tax authority. In that correspondence, an unresolved tax claim against the subsidiary comes to light, and it is nowhere in the seller's disclosure. The lawyers then write a two-page memo, with the recommendation in the very first line. The board approves new terms: a lower price, money held in escrow, and a specific indemnity. Finally, after two weeks of resistance, the seller accepts, and the closing date moves from March to May.
